plain: TABOR, a 1992 state constitutional limit, makes Colorado refund tax money collected above a cap. Proposition NN would let the state keep that extra money, up to a higher cap, for schools and children’s programs.

short_version.text: Proposition NN trades refunds for school money. For the next two years, refunds would drop to zero; for a single filer with $50,000 to $100,000 of income that is about $21 to $68 a year. Schools and children's programs would get about $240 million a year each at first, and possibly far more later.

connection.text: NN is about what happens to money the state collects above its TABOR limit: refund it, or keep it for schools and children's programs. Later refunds are unknown and could be zero in some years or over $1,000 per taxpayer in others.

agree_means: Agreeing means voting yes on Proposition NN. TABOR refunds would stop for at least two years and likely several more, and the money would go to K-12 schools and children’s programs.
disagree_means: Disagreeing means voting no. Refunds continue under current law whenever revenue tops the cap, and the state balances its budget without this money.

research_notes: No source in this file needed the browser. For a reviewer: (1) Older NN numbers circulated: Colorado Politics (July 17, 2026) quoted $136.1M for 2026-27 and $969.7M for 2027-28 from an earlier analysis, and an April 2026 analysis requested by Sen. Kirkmeyer said $7,381 per taxpayer over 10 years with about 24 percent to K-12, based on an earlier version of SB26-135 before it was amended. I used the final Blue Book and the June 2026 Legislative Council forecast ($329.9M and $521.0M) and flagged the older figures in unknowns. (2) Blue Book Table 1 refunds assume the standard deduction and are by tax year; the table-row quotes may not match the checker's PDF extraction. Per-year numbers come from that table; the Common Sense Institute page gives two-year single-filer totals ($60, $96, $341) that match the sums. (3) The CSI full PDF for NN returned 404; I quoted its web summary (Aug. 6, 2026). Its job loss range spans two scenarios (new state spending does or does not create public jobs). (4) Not used: Yes for Colorado Kids' claim of up to 50 percent more K-12 funding (campaign claim) and the 'slush fund' framing of the earlier bill.
